name: Battle of Mons-en-Pévèle
summary: Philip IV of France avenges the humiliation of Courtrai (1302) at the Battle of Mons-en-Pévèle on August 18, 1304. The Flemish infantry, which had destroyed the French knights at Courtrai, is this time outmaneuvered; the French cavalry finds terrain suitable for mounted attack and breaks the Flemish lines. The Treaty of Athis-sur-Orge (1305) imposes heavy reparations on Flanders and partial French control. The battle demonstrates that Courtrai was not a universal tactical revolution, infantry could still be defeated by determined and well-led cavalry.

_quarry.structural_significance: Restores French prestige after Courtrai; the peace terms reimpose French overlordship on Flanders; the Flemish towns' wealth and strategic position make them a perpetual source of Anglo-French conflict, Edward III's alliance with Flanders (1337) is a direct trigger of the Hundred Years' War; the wool trade between England and Flemish weavers creates the economic interdependency that complicates the war
